analysis.one_liner: Strips bank and market reporting rules, requires warrants for financial records, and lets Congress veto financial regulations.
analysis.headline: The Saving Privacy Act, introduced by Senator Mike Lee with one cosponsor, has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since February 2025 with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rebuild the rules around financial surveillance: government agencies could generally only get someone's bank records with a warrant, banks and payment platforms would report far less customer activity, and the database that tracks stock market trades would be shut down. It would also ban a government digital dollar, protect self-custodied cryptocurrency wallets, and require a vote of Congress before major rules from financial regulators — including rules already in effect — could stay on the books. Some of this gives everyday people genuine privacy; the same text also tears down the reporting system used to trace money laundering, terrorism financing, and market manipulation.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and payment companies that currently spend heavily on federal reporting; crypto holders and platforms; casual sellers who would no longer receive tax forms for small online sales; and anyone who wants their financial records shielded from federal agencies without a warrant. Users of hard-to-trace corporate entities also benefit, since the bill drops beneficial-ownership reporting.

how_it_helps.text: Bars federal agencies from accessing a person's financial records without a search warrant meeting Fourth Amendment standards, and adds criminal penalties (fines up to $5,000 and up to 5 years in prison) plus civil penalties of at least $1,000 per violation per day for agencies or banks that obtain or disclose records improperly.

Eliminates the current rules requiring banks to file reports on large transactions and suspicious activity with the federal government; under the bill those records could only be obtained through a search warrant.

Restores the pre-2022 threshold so payment platforms only report transactions when a person exceeds $20,000 and 200 transactions in a year, sparing casual sellers from receiving tax forms for small online sales.

Prohibits federal agencies from restricting a person's use of cryptocurrency to buy goods and services for their own use or to transact through a self-hosted wallet, and prohibits agencies from issuing or using a central bank digital currency.

Requires Congress to pass a joint resolution approving major rules (those with roughly $100 million or more in annual economic effect) issued by financial regulators including the Fed, SEC, CFTC, FDIC, CFPB, Treasury, and credit union regulator before they take effect, and starts a process that sunsets existing rules not approved by Congress within five years.

analysis.who_pays: The costs fall on the other side of the same coin: investigators lose the routine records they use to trace money laundering, terrorism financing, fraud, and market manipulation; tax enforcement of unreported online income gets harder; and rules protecting bank customers and investors could lapse unless Congress affirmatively votes to keep each one.

drawbacks.text: Eliminates the Bank Secrecy Act reporting that currently helps detect money laundering and terrorism financing — including reports on transfers over $10,000 — meaning those records could only be obtained case-by-case through a search warrant.

Orders the SEC to terminate the Consolidated Audit Trail, the centralized database national securities exchanges built to track market activity and detect manipulation, and bars agencies from creating any similar centralized database of Americans' personal information without a specific new law.
Eliminates or reduces reporting of the beneficial ownership of certain corporate entities, the records that show who actually owns a company.

Under the congressional-review provisions, major financial rules — including rules already in effect — can only survive if Congress affirmatively votes to approve them; rules not approved within five years cease to have effect, which could unravel large parts of existing financial regulation through sheer congressional inaction.

Even supporters would acknowledge that gutting suspicious-activity and beneficial-ownership reporting cuts both ways: the same records that feel like surveillance also let investigators follow dirty money through banks, shell companies, and securities markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy provisions are real: a warrant requirement for financial records, protection for self-custodied crypto, and the 1099-K fix respond to burdens people genuinely feel. But the bill attaches those provisions to the wholesale dismantling of the financial reporting system — routine transaction reports, suspicious activity reports, beneficial ownership, and the market audit trail — and to a congressional-veto regime that could let existing financial rules lapse without any vote. For ordinary people, the gains are modest and the lost enforcement and oversight are large, so the trade is a bad one as written.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2025, and the committee has taken no further action on it.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Lee introduced the Saving Privacy Act in the Senate on February 27, 2025, joined by Senator Rick Scott of Florida.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, where it has remained since.

The bill would end or cut back requirements that financial institutions report customer transactions, require warrants for federal access to financial records, terminate the Consolidated Audit Trail, ban a central bank digital currency, and require congressional approval for major financial rules including some currently in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet — the bill has not moved, so banks, crypto users, and regulators all continue operating under existing rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No change yet — status quo holds

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill combining financial-privacy reforms, crypto protections, a ban on a central bank digital currency, and congressional approval of financial regulators' rules.

for.name: Sen. Rick Scott
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only senator to sign on alongside the sponsor.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral the day it was introduced and has never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: So far only two Republican senators support the bill — Mike Lee and Rick Scott — no Democrats have signed on, and no vote has occurred to show how the parties would split.

industries.note: The bill removes the Bank Secrecy Act reporting duties that banks must perform today, cutting their compliance burden, while also barring government access to their customers' records without a warrant. The cost for the public is that regulators lose the routine records used to catch money laundering and fraud. [S2, S3]

The bill bars agencies from restricting personal use of cryptocurrency or self-hosted wallets and prohibits any government digital dollar, giving crypto users protection from federal control that many in the industry have sought. [S2, S3]

Shutting down the Consolidated Audit Trail ends the centralized record of market activity that regulators built to detect manipulation and misconduct; trading firms stop paying CAT fees (and existing ones must be reimbursed). Investors lose the surveillance tool that helps catch market abuse. [S2, S3]

industries.industry: Anonymous shell companies and their formation agents
industries.note: The bill eliminates or reduces beneficial-ownership reporting, so the people behind certain corporate entities would no longer be recorded — which benefits those who use such entities to hide ownership and weakens investigators' ability to trace dirty money. [S2]

Restoring the $20,000-and-200-transactions threshold means platforms stop issuing tax forms for small sellers' transactions, a fix that casual sellers and the platforms themselves both favor, though it also makes unreported income easier. [S3]

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, one cosponsor, and no committee action more than a year into the 119th Congress, the bill is likely to die quietly in the Senate Finance Committee unless pieces of it are attached to a larger moving bill; its individual elements (the 1099-K threshold, the CAT, anti-CBDC language) tend to advance separately rather than as this package.
